why_how.text: Careless driving or certain law violations can lead to suspension, cancellation or revocation even before a person has received a license.
Idaho maintains crash and moving-violation records, including out-of-state events, for people who have never received a license as well as licensed drivers.
The handbook identifies Idaho as a Driver License Compact member and describes the compact as promoting compliance across member states.
Under the described compact, serious offenses and minor moving violations go to the driver's home state for treatment as a home-state violation.
A licensed Idaho driver's out-of-state traffic conviction is added to the Idaho record, with suspension if the offense is suspendable.
The handbook's moving-violation point scale assigns one through four points per recorded violation.
The point table lists a warning letter for eight through eleven points within any twelve months.
The point table lists a thirty-day suspension for twelve through seventeen points within any twelve months.
The point table lists a ninety-day suspension for eighteen through twenty-three points within any twenty-four months.
The point table lists a six-month suspension for at least twenty-four points within any thirty-six months.
The handbook permits point removal once in three years through an approved defensive-driving course or the described law-enforcement traffic course.
Those point-removal courses reduce points but do not remove the conviction from the driving record.
Completing an ITD-approved defensive-driving course can remove at most three points, and the points must already be recorded before the course is completed.

Unlawful license or identification-card use, lack of required vehicle insurance and violating a license restriction appear among the listed grounds.
The source also lists school-compliance failures, unpaid child support, visitation noncompliance and failure to obey a paternity-suit subpoena.

title.text: Keep GDL and ALS conditions distinct

why_how.text: For drivers younger than seventeen, the first moving-violation conviction brings the handbook's warning letter.
For drivers younger than seventeen, a second moving-violation conviction carries a thirty-day driving suspension.
For drivers younger than seventeen, a third or later moving-violation conviction carries a sixty-day suspension.
The described GDL penalties are additional to supervised-instruction permit cancellation or other court or department suspensions.
The GDL penalty periods are absolute and allow no driving privileges of any kind.

After a DUI arrest and an evidentiary result over the legal alcohol limit, an officer serves an immediate suspension notice; a notice may instead be sent after blood or urine results establish the described intoxication.
The described ALS is an administrative suspension imposed by the transportation department under the cited alcohol-test law.
The handbook allows an ALS hearing request within seven days of the date written on the suspension notice, before a department-designated hearing officer.

why_how.text: An ALS is a civil sanction separate from criminal court penalties; its requirements do not remove the duty to attend the scheduled DUI court appearance.
The handbook makes the suspension notice effective thirty days after service, meaning receipt of the notice.
For a first evidentiary-test failure, the handbook gives a ninety-day suspension with no driving during its first thirty days.
After that first-failure suspension ends, the source requires an ignition interlock on any vehicle driven for one year.
A second evidentiary-test failure within five years carries a one-year suspension allowing no driving privileges.
The handbook's implied-consent description covers a person driving or physically controlling a vehicle when suspected of impaired driving, for an alcohol or drug test under the stated law.
Refusing an officer-requested evidentiary test subjects the person to the described suspension and a two-hundred-fifty-dollar civil penalty.
For the described first refusal, an officer issues a notice and a court's upholding the findings leads to a one-year absolute suspension.
A second test refusal within ten years brings a two-year absolute suspension in addition to any DUI-conviction penalty.
